problem: VLM-based place (room) recognition hallucinates confidently, and ambiguous human instructions make it worse. Prior uncertainty handling relies on prompt-engineered confidence (Prompt Set, Binary Set) or always trusts the top-1 prediction, and KnowNo-style uncertainty alignment has not been applied to open-vocabulary room classification.
motivation: Assistive robots for people with disabilities must recognize rooms reliably and ask for help only when needed, since over-asking is costly and wrong guesses are unsafe. Statistical guarantees from conformal prediction can calibrate when the robot should ask, replacing unreliable LLM self-reported uncertainty.
key_idea: Apply split conformal prediction to VLM (LongCLIP) image-text similarity scores to build calibrated prediction sets of candidate rooms, and ask the human for clarification only when the set has more than one room.
insight: LLM-generated prediction sets are hallucinated and biased toward the first listed options, whereas CP sets calibrated on similarity scores give a flexible, continuous trade-off between success and help rate. At the Prompt Set's normalized set size (0.13), CP reaches 53% success vs 18%. At a matched help rate of about 15%, CP reaches about 31% success vs about 19% for Prompt Set. These are read from plots, and the paper has no ablations.
method: Description extraction: an LLM, via prompt engineering, extracts a room description from the user's instruction.
Calibration data: LLaVA generates descriptions of top-down room images. The pairs are split into a VLM fine-tuning part and a CP calibration part.
VLM scoring: fine-tuned LongCLIP computes cosine similarity between the description and each candidate top-down room image.
Non-conformity score: 1 minus the similarity of the true-label pair, computed over ranked candidates, inspired by the Oracle algorithm of Gibbs et al.
Conformal calibration: q-hat is the ceil((n+1)(1-alpha))/n quantile of calibration scores, giving coverage of at least 1-alpha.
Prediction set and help trigger: candidates with score at most q-hat form the set. If the set contains more than one room, the robot asks the user for clarification (help rate = 1).

setting.backbone: LongCLIP (fine-tuned) for text-image matching; LLaVA to generate room descriptions; an LLM for description extraction
setting.training_data: Matterport3D top-down room images with LLaVA-generated descriptions; a subset of scenes is used to fine-tune LongCLIP and another subset for CP calibration
setting.observation: top-down view images of rooms plus a text description
setting.action_space: none (room selection / prediction set plus a help request; no navigation actions)
setting.privileged: none (room segmentation from the dataset is used to define the candidate rooms)

numbers_note: Results are given only in figures (success rate vs set size and help rate) and in the text as approximate values; there are no tables and no standard navigation benchmark. Text values: at set size 0.13 CP gets 53% success vs Prompt Set 18%; at equal help CP gets 31% vs Prompt Set ~19%; No Help ~12%.
results: On 43 Matterport3D test scenes (1504 rooms), CP yields 53% success vs 18% for Prompt Set at the same normalized set size of 0.13. At a matched help rate CP reaches about 31% vs about 19% for Prompt Set. It also gives a continuous trade-off that Binary Set (100% help for perfect success) and No Help (~12% success) cannot.
limitations: Evaluated only offline on Matterport3D with LLaVA-generated descriptions, so test and calibration data are same-distribution; no real-robot or real user instructions.
Results appear only in plots and success is low at small set sizes; the paper does not compare against stronger baselines and has no ablations.
Discussion section text appears copied from a different (shared-autonomy navigation) paper. The abstract's 'no fine-tuning' claim conflicts with the method, which fine-tunes LongCLIP.
